summary: The direct object — what is eaten, drunk, bought, liked or cooked — comes after the verb. Hebrew nouns have no case endings, but a **definite** direct object gets the small word אֶת (et) in front of it: הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ “he eats an apple” — הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ “he eats the apple”. Definite means: a noun with הַ, a two-word noun whose second word has הַ (אֶת אֲרוּחַת הַבֹּקֶר), a noun with הַ + שֶׁלִּי … or הַזֶּה (אֶת הַקָּפֶה שֶׁלּוֹ), a name, or a pronoun. An indefinite object has no marker at all. אֶת is not translated; it does the job of an accusative, but only for a definite object, and the noun after it never changes. With a pronoun אֶת takes endings: אוֹתִי “me”, אוֹתוֹ “him, it”, אוֹתָהּ “her, it” … In standard Hebrew the thing after יֵשׁ / אֵין is a subject, so it has no אֶת. Objects with prepositions (to, for, with) and the indirect object come later (S11–S13, C03).

blocks.title: אֶת = “the following object is definite”
blocks.text: Hebrew marks the direct object only when it is definite: הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ “he eats an apple” / הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ “he eats the apple”. The noun itself is the same in both.

blocks.title: No אֶת before an indefinite object
blocks.text: *הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת תַּפּוּחַ is wrong: without הַ there is no אֶת — הוּא אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ.

blocks.title: אֶת or אַתְּ?
blocks.text: Without vowel marks both are written את: אֶת (et) marks the object, אַתְּ (at) is “you” to a woman. The sentence tells you which: אַתְּ אוֹכֶלֶת אֶת הַלֶּחֶם “you (f.) eat the bread”.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: What is eaten, drunk, bought, liked?
Does it have הַ, a name, a pronoun?

askYourself: Does the verb have a direct object (what is eaten, drunk, bought, liked, cooked)?
Is the object definite — with הַ, a definite second word, a name, a pronoun? → אֶת before it.
Is it indefinite (no article)? → nothing before it.
Is it a pronoun? → אֶת with an ending: אוֹתוֹ, אוֹתָהּ …
Is it after יֵשׁ / אֵין? → standard Hebrew puts no אֶת there.
Is there a preposition (to, with, for)? → that is not a direct object (S11).
steps: Definite object: אֶת + the definite noun.

traps: *הוּא אוֹכֵל אֶת תַּפּוּחַ — אֶת only before a definite object.
*אֲנִי אוֹהֵב הַסָּלָט — a definite object needs אֶת: אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הַסָּלָט.
In a two-word noun הַ goes on the second word, but אֶת stands before the whole: אֶת אֲרוּחַת הָעֶרֶב.
*אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הוּא — the object pronoun is one word: אוֹתוֹ.
אֶת “(object)” and אַתְּ “you (f.)” look the same without vowels: את.
The subject never takes אֶת: הַיֶּלֶד אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ.

seeAlso.note: Arabic marks every direct object with the accusative ending -a / -an (أَكَلَ التُّفَّاحَةَ, أَكَلَ تُفَّاحَةً), definite or not; Hebrew marks only the definite one, and with a separate word, אֶת.
German puts every direct object in the accusative, seen mostly on the article (einen Apfel / den Apfel); Hebrew adds אֶת only before a definite object.
Chinese has no object marker here: word order alone (我吃苹果) shows the object.

notes.text: It works like the Turkish accusative: only a definite (specific) object is marked — elma yiyorum / elmayı yiyorum ~ אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ / אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ. But אֶת is a separate word before the noun, not a suffix.
Greek marks every direct object with the accusative (έναν / τον), definite or not; Hebrew marks only a definite one, with אֶת: אוֹכֵל תַּפּוּחַ / אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ.
Russian changes the ending of every object (книгу), definite or not; Hebrew changes nothing in the noun and puts אֶת only before a definite object.
Spanish a marks a personal object (veo a Juan); Hebrew אֶת marks a definite object, person or thing (אֲנִי אוֹהֵב אֶת הַסָּלָט) — and never an indefinite one.
English has no object marker for nouns; Hebrew puts אֶת before a definite object (אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ “eats the apple”). It is not translated.
French has no object marker; Hebrew adds אֶת before a definite object, as if to say “the following object is definite”.
German marks every direct object with the accusative (einen / den Apfel); Hebrew marks only the definite one, with אֶת, and the noun never changes.
Hindi को marks a definite or human object (लड़के को देखा), much as אֶת marks a definite one; but को follows the noun, and אֶת comes before it.
Persian را after a definite object (سیب را می‌خورم) is the mirror image of אֶת before it (אוֹכֵל אֶת הַתַּפּוּחַ).
Arabic marks every object with the accusative ending (أَكَلَ تُفَّاحَةً / التُّفَّاحَةَ); Hebrew lost the endings and marks only a definite object, with אֶת.
Japanese を marks every direct object, after it (りんごを食べる); Hebrew אֶת marks only a definite object, and stands before it.
Korean 을 / 를 marks any object, after it; Hebrew אֶת marks only a definite object, before it.
Finnish chooses between the partitive and the total object by completeness (syön omenaa / syön omenan); Hebrew chooses by definiteness: אֶת or nothing.
Hungarian marks every object with -t but changes the verb when the object is definite (eszek egy almát / eszem az almát); Hebrew marks the definite object with אֶת and leaves the verb alone.
Swahili can repeat a known object as a marker inside the verb; Hebrew never puts the object in the verb — it uses אֶת, or אוֹתוֹ for a pronoun.
Luganda puts object pronouns inside the verb (amulaba “he sees him”); Hebrew uses a separate word: אוֹתוֹ “him” = אֶת + an ending.
Chinese marks no object (把 can move a definite one before the verb); Hebrew keeps the object after the verb and adds אֶת when it is definite.
Vietnamese marks no object; Hebrew adds אֶת before a definite one.

Inuktitut also separates definite objects: they go with a transitive verb ending, while an indefinite object takes the ending -mik with an intransitive verb; Hebrew marks the definite object with אֶת and leaves the verb alone.
